summary: Suggests a simple way to deliver one-way alphanumeric and numeric pages to radio paging terminals. It is informational and describes version 1(b). It was replaced by RFC 1645.

eli5.summary: A pager is a small box that beeps with a message. This memo is a simple way to send those short messages over the Internet.

questions: how to send pages to a pager over the internet
how to send a page over the internet
difference between snpp and email for paging
subtitle: A simple protocol for delivering alphanumeric and numeric pages to pagers over the Internet.

tldr.problem: Sending pages to pagers required complex protocols and dedicated modems, making it difficult to deliver pages from computers over the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: SNPP (Simple Network Paging Protocol) provides a straightforward command-response system where clients connect to a paging gateway, specify a pager ID and message, and send the page.
tldr.outcome: Pages can be sent reliably and immediately from the Internet to pagers without needing a modem or complex protocols, though it was replaced by more flexible approaches.

facts.label: Main commands
facts.value: 6: PAGE, MESS, SEND, RESET, QUIT, HELP

today: RFC 1568 is obsoleted by RFC 1645. SNPP represents an informational approach to urgent paging over the Internet, now superseded by other methods. The IETF recommended email-based approaches instead, though the simple command-response design of SNPP influenced later protocols.

sections.title: The Problem with Traditional Paging
sections.content:
Radio pagers have been popular for sending short urgent messages, but traditionally they required a modem and specialized software to reach. SNPP (Simple Network Paging Protocol) was designed to let Internet-connected computers send pages directly to pagers without needing modems or complex setup.

The RFC notes that email, while reliable, has a fundamental problem for urgent paging: messages can be delayed if a gateway is down, and the sender may not find out about the delay immediately. A real-time paging protocol solves this by giving instant feedback about whether the message was accepted by the paging network.
sections.eli5: Pagers are good for urgent messages, but it was hard to send them from computers. SNPP lets you send a page right away and know right away if it worked or not, which is better than email that might get stuck in a queue.

sections.title: The SNPP Design
sections.content:
SNPP is intentionally simple, following the philosophy of other Internet protocols. The protocol is built on a sequence of commands and replies, with six main commands that clients can send and responses that fall into three categories: successful, failed but continue, and failed with disconnection.

The server response code's first digit indicates the category: 2xx for success, 5xx for continued failure, and 4xx for failure with termination. This pattern is borrowed from SMTP and similar protocols, making it familiar to implementers.

The design isolates the details of the underlying TAP/IXO paging protocol (which is complex) from users and from software that might later support different paging networks. This makes SNPP a clean interface that can adapt as paging technology evolves.
sections.eli5: SNPP uses simple typed commands like other Internet protocols. The server answers with a number code that tells you if things worked, are still happening, or failed. It hides all the complicated stuff that pagers actually need to do.

sections.title: SNPP Commands
sections.content:
The client uses six commands to communicate with an SNPP server. The PAGE command sets the pager ID (the number to page). The MESS command sets the message text, either alphanumeric or numeric. The SEND command processes the page, checking that both the pager ID and message are present, then forwarding them to the paging network.

The RESET command clears the pager ID and message, letting the user start over. The QUIT command terminates the session. The optional HELP command displays information about valid commands, useful for manual telnet sessions.

If a required field is missing before SEND, the server responds with an error but keeps the connection open. Duplicate PAGEr or MESSage commands are rejected with an error that indicates information was already entered. Illegal commands cause immediate disconnection or a recoverable error depending on server configuration.
sections.eli5: You send commands to the server: PAGE to say who to page, MESS to say what to send, SEND to actually page them, RESET to start over, and QUIT to leave. HELP is available if you need to know the commands.

sections.title: A Typical Session
sections.content:
A typical successful connection starts when the client opens a connection, and the server responds with a greeting and "250 READY". The client sends a PAGEr command with a pager ID, the server responds "250 OK". The client sends a MESSage command with the message text, and the server again responds "250 OK".

The client then issues SEND, and the server forwards the message to the TAP/IXO paging terminal, waits for a response, and reports back. A successful send receives "250 Page Sent". Failures might be "550 Failed, Illegal Pager ID" or "554 Failed, <reason>". After sending, the server stays connected to allow the client to send another page. Finally, the client sends QUIT, and the server responds "221 OK, Goodbye" and closes.

This simple flow makes SNPP easy to use both programmatically and manually via telnet, a design goal stated in the RFC.
sections.eli5: You connect, the server says it is ready. You tell it the pager number, it says okay. You tell it the message, it says okay. You say SEND, it pages them and tells you if it worked. You say QUIT and the connection closes.

sections.title: Status and Obsolescence
sections.content:
RFC 1568 was published in January 1994 as an Informational RFC. It has been obsoleted by RFC 1645. The IETF reviewed SNPP and concluded that extending SMTP or using the existing email infrastructure was preferable, citing the costs of deploying a new protocol.

Despite its obsolescence, SNPP demonstrated an important approach: a lightweight protocol optimized for a specific real-time task. The RFC acknowledged that while it was informational and experimental, similar protocols and design patterns continue to appear in Internet applications.
sections.eli5: SNPP was replaced by a newer version (RFC 1645). The IETF preferred using email instead, but SNPP showed a useful way to handle urgent, real-time tasks that email cannot handle well.
